strengths: Timely and practically motivated problem: addressing how intrinsic MoE routing properties affect expert offloading efficiency on memory-constrained devices.
Comprehensive empirical study: analyzes 20 distinct MoE architectures and scales (ranging from 3B to 57B parameters), providing extensive coverage of open-weight MoE models.
Well-formulated metrics: SRP is derived with an exact optimization threshold and provides a parameter-free characterization, while SCH directly links routing consistency to real-world cache limits.

Valuable design and deployment insights: demonstrates that domain specialization drives routing consistency more than vocabulary specialization, that shared experts/dense layers can dilute consistency, and identifies a 2x active expert cache capacity as an effective operational sweet spot.
weaknesses: Lack of end-to-end runtime evaluations: While cache hit rates and correlations with LRU/LFU are demonstrated, the paper does not measure actual wall-clock latency, tokens-per-second throughput, or PCIe transfer overheads on hardware testbeds running offloading systems (e.g., Fiddler or MoE-Infinity).

Correlation vs. causation in architecture takeaways: Observations regarding the negative impact of shared experts and hybrid dense-MoE layers are derived post-hoc across existing models with varying pretraining datasets and training objectives, rather than controlled ablation pretraining experiments.

Relatively short context window evaluation: Sequences are chunked into 512 tokens to accommodate older models like SwitchTransformers, which may not capture routing consistency behaviors over long contexts (e.g., 4k–32k tokens) typical of modern LLM workloads.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis covering a wide spectrum of 20 modern open-source MoE LLMs across diverse parameter scales (3B to 57B) and architectural variants.
Formulation of two well-motivated and mathematically defined metrics (SRP and SCH) that rigorously quantify local routing consistency at both the individual expert and layer/model levels.

Interesting analytical findings regarding expert behavior, including the observation that domain specialization correlates much more strongly with routing locality than vocabulary specialization, and that local consistency does not necessarily preclude load balancing.
Extensive appendix providing proofs for metric maximization, layer-wise trends, transitivity across domains, and base vs. post-trained model comparisons.
weaknesses: The study is entirely observational and simulation-based; it lacks end-to-end hardware profiling (e.g., wall-clock latency, tokens/sec, transfer overheads in actual GPU-to-CPU or GPU-to-NVMe offloading pipelines) to demonstrate whether the measured differences in SCH translate to meaningful real-world speedups.

Architectural insights are somewhat one-sided regarding modeling capacity: recommending the removal of shared experts or avoiding dense layers solely for offloading locality disregards why modern architectures (such as DeepSeek-V2/V3) adopt them, namely significant gains in training stability and modeling quality per active parameter.

SRP and SCH metrics can be heavily inflated by expert collapse or severe routing imbalance (as seen in LLaMA-MoE-v2 and Yuan2.0), making high consistency partially an artifact of pathological router behavior rather than purely desirable locality.

The analysis relies on concatenated 512-token sequences evaluated in teacher-forcing / forward-pass mode; it does not analyze whether autoregressive generation dynamics (e.g., open-ended generation, reasoning chains) exhibit the exact same routing consistency.
Clear signs of unpolished drafting, most notably the abstract ending abruptly with an incomplete sentence ('We publish the code for replicating experiments a').

strengths: Timely and important topic: While many MoE offloading systems implicitly rely on token-level activation locality, this work provides the first comprehensive, systematic audit quantifying 'local routing consistency' across modern MoE models.

Extensive empirical study: The paper evaluates 20 open-source MoE LLMs spanning diverse parameter scales (3B to 57B) and architectural paradigms (varying expert granularities, shared experts, and layer interleaving).

Principled metric formulation: Segment Routing Best Performance (SRP) and Segment Cache Best Hit Rate (SCH) are well-defined mathematically, accompanied by clear analytical proofs in the appendix demonstrating their optimality properties.

Actionable insights: The paper reveals valuable design observations, notably that dense shared modules dilute routing consistency, domain specialization helps reconcile consistency with load balance, and a cache size ratio of ~2x active experts serves as an empirical sweet spot.
Strong validation of oracle metrics: The authors validate that SCH strongly correlates with practical online caching algorithms (LRU, LFU, and fixed cache) across multiple segment lengths.
weaknesses: Lack of end-to-end runtime/latency evaluation: The evaluation is purely metric-driven (F1 and cache hit rate). The paper lacks wall-clock speedup and inference latency measurements on actual offloading setups (e.g., CPU-GPU or NVMe-GPU offloading) to verify whether higher consistency directly translates to real serving speedups under memory bandwidth constraints.

Correlational rather than causal architecture findings: The conclusion that 'no shared experts' and 'MoE on every layer' maximize consistency is drawn purely from observational comparisons across pre-trained models that differ in training data, auxiliary routing loss weights, and optimization objectives. Controlled pre-training ablations would be needed to prove causality.

Distinction between prefilling and autoregressive decoding: The analysis evaluates sequences processed forward in chunks of 512 tokens. While routing consistency is relevant across both phases, offloading bottlenecks differ vastly between parallel prefill and sequential decoding; a more distinct breakdown would strengthen practical relevance.
Minor presentation flaw: The last sentence of the abstract is cut off ('We publish the code for replicating experiments a').

strengths: Timely and practically important research topic: with the rapid proliferation of open-source MoE models on edge and resource-constrained devices, understanding what model properties enable efficient expert caching/offloading is of high interest to both model designers and systems researchers.

Extensive empirical study: the paper evaluates 20 diverse real-world open-weight MoE LLMs (ranging from 3B to 57B parameters, covering varying architectures such as shared experts, deep/shallow routing, and different granularity) alongside a controlled suite of 1.43B toy MoE models trained from scratch to systematically isolate individual design factors.

Sound and well-formulated metrics: SRP (Segment Routing Best Performance) and SCH (Segment Cache Best Hit Rate) are mathematically well-grounded, with rigorous proofs for optimal activation thresholds provided in the appendix, offering clean abstractions that isolate routing consistency from specific cache replacement implementations.

Insightful architectural takeaways: the paper uncovers meaningful findings, such as the trade-off between local routing consistency and local load balance, how shared experts can inadvertently harm routing consistency by constraining the combination space, and how domain specialization (rather than vocabulary specialization) enables both global load balance and high local routing consistency.
weaknesses: Gap between analytical cache hit rate metrics and end-to-end system throughput: while SCH correlates well with LRU/LFU cache hit rates, the actual connection to hardware wall-clock latency and memory bus bottlenecks (e.g., PCIe transfer overhead vs. compute overlap) is only discussed briefly in Appendix F, where the observed decoding throughput correlation is modest (r ≈ -0.3).

Heuristic nature of the '2x active experts' rule: the claim that a cache size of ~2x active experts represents an optimal balance relies largely on qualitative observation of the 'elbow' in SCH curves rather than hardware-aware performance-per-watt or latency Pareto frontier analysis across different device bandwidth regimes.

Visual presentation and figure readability: several figures (e.g., Figures 4, 6, 7, and 8) are overly dense, with overlapping text labels that are difficult to interpret without extreme zooming. Additionally, the emojis in Figure 1 appear informal for a top-tier venue publication.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 20 diverse MoE LLMs (spanning sizes from 3B to 57B and various architectures such as Mixtral, DeepSeek-V2, Qwen, OLMoE, SwitchTransformers).

Controlled ablation using a suite of toy models trained from scratch to systematically isolate the impact of architecture hyperparameters (e.g., shared experts, load balance loss coefficient, expert granularity, combination space).

Clear mathematical formulation of Segment Routing Best Performance (SRP) with complete proofs demonstrating the existence of an optimal segment activation threshold, alongside Segment Cache Best Hit Rate (SCH) that bridges theory to caching setups.

Insightful findings that explain the tension between local load balance and local routing consistency, as well as the detrimental impact of shared experts on caching efficiency due to restricted combination spaces.
Detailed analysis of domain-wise vs. vocabulary-wise specialization and its impact on routing stability across contexts.
weaknesses: The evaluation primarily centers on theoretical caching metrics (F1-bound and hit rate) rather than end-to-end inference latency or wall-clock throughput on realistic heterogeneous hardware (CPU-GPU offloading). While Appendix F touches upon throughput, the correlation with decoding speed is moderate (r ≈ -0.3).

Some high-SRP phenomena appear to be byproducts of pathologically imbalanced models (e.g., LLaMA-MoE-v2 collapses onto a small set of experts), making high consistency partially an artifact of poor expert utilization rather than an inherently desirable property unless balanced globally.
Visual presentation in certain figures (e.g., Figure 1 styling, dense annotations and font sizes in Figures 4, 6, 7, and 14–18) is quite cramped and could be improved for readability.

strengths: Important and timely research question: While many MoE offloading frameworks rely on the assumption of temporal routing locality, this work systematically evaluates whether that assumption holds across modern MoE architectures.

The proposed metrics, Segment Routing Best Performance (SRP) and Segment Cache Best Hit Rate (SCH), are theoretically grounded (with formal proofs of optimal bounds provided in the appendix) and parameter-free, effectively capturing both intrinsic routing consistency and practical offloading bounds.
Comprehensive empirical study evaluating 20 open MoE models spanning different sizes, families, and architectures (e.g., Mixtral, OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2, Qwen-MoE, Switch Transformers).

Methodologically rigorous ablation using custom-pretrained 1.43B toy models trained on 20B tokens to isolate confounding architectural factors (such as load balancing loss, shared experts, and expert combination space), providing causal evidence for the empirical observations.

Actionable and insightful conclusions for both model designers and systems researchers, including the trade-off between local and global load balance, the detrimental effect of shared experts on routing consistency, and the identification of 2x active experts as an empirical sweet spot for offloading caches.
weaknesses: The empirical validation primarily revolves around analytical metrics (SRP/SCH) and simulated cache hit rates (LRU/LFU/optimal), with actual end-to-end systems benchmarking (wall-clock latency and throughput on real memory-constrained hardware/offloading runtimes) relegated to a preliminary analysis in Appendix F on toy models.

While the paper analyzes the trade-off between routing consistency and perplexity on 1.43B toy models, the question of whether explicitly training for routing consistency impacts scaling efficiency or downstream reasoning capabilities at larger scales remains an open question.

Several high-level recommendations (e.g., caching roughly 2x the number of active experts) are relatively well-known heuristics in systems literature, although this work formalizes and unifies the underlying reasons across multiple models.
